passage.text: Balance between asymmetric allocation and repair of somatic damage in unicellular life forms as an ancient form of r/K selection
Significance

Somatic damage accumulation is an inevitable consequence of cellular metabolism, yet the environmental and physiological determinants of optimal strategy for coping with this damage remain poorly understood. Prior work focused on models assuming damage accumulation is linear. We demonstrate that relaxing this assumption results in substantially more complex dynamics giving rise to three distinct damage control strategies involving both the repair and asymmetric allocation of somatic damage. Which of these strategies is optimal strongly depends on extrinsic mortality, consistent with the interpretation that the balance of repair and asymmetry represents an r/K selection regime. At an early stage of life evolution, this trade-off might have given rise to the first specialized r and K strategists and morphologically asymmetric cell division.

Over the course of multiple divisions, cells accumulate diverse nongenetic, somatic damage including misfolded and aggregated proteins and cell wall defects. If the rate of damage accumulation exceeds the rate of dilution through cell growth, a dedicated mitigation strategy is required to prevent eventual population collapse. Strategies for somatic damage control can be divided into two categories, asymmetric allocation and repair, which are not, in principle, mutually exclusive. We explore a mathematical model to identify the optimal strategy, maximizing the total cell number, over a wide range of environmental and physiological conditions. The optimal strategy is primarily determined by extrinsic, damage-independent mortality and the physiological model for damage accumulation that can be either independent (linear) or increasing (exponential) with respect to the prior accumulated damage. Under the linear regime, the optimal strategy is either exclusively repair or asymmetric allocation, whereas under the exponential regime, the optimal strategy is a combination of asymmetry and repair. Repair is preferred when extrinsic mortality is low, whereas at high extrinsic mortality, asymmetric damage allocation becomes the strategy of choice. We hypothesize that at an early stage of life evolution, optimization over repair and asymmetric allocation of somatic damage gave rise to r and K selection strategists.

Over the course of multiple divisions, cells accumulate two types of damage, genetic and somatic. Somatic damage includes the deterioration of all cellular components other than genomic DNA, including RNA, proteins, and other macromolecular structures, such as cell walls. Perhaps the most common form of somatic damage is the accumulation of misfolded proteins in the cytoplasm. Somatic damage, like genetic damage, is heritable across cell divisions but is not copied prior to its distribution among daughter cells. Also, like genetic damage, which, in the absence of dedicated mitigation, leads to the eventual collapse of asexual populations through Muller’s ratchet, somatic damage will lead to collapse when damage accumulates faster than it is diluted through cell growth and division.

Somatic damage mitigation strategies can be roughly divided into two categories: i) asymmetric damage allocation and ii) repair, which are not, in principle, mutually exclusive. Repair involves the synthesis of replacement materials for essential machinery [e.g., correcting cell wall defects ]; degradation of damaged components within the cell into reusable materials [e.g., proteolytic degradation of misfolded proteins ]; or extrusion of dysfunctional material (e.g., misfolded protein aggregates) into the external environment. All these are active strategies, requiring variable energy investment. The most widespread mechanism of somatic damage repair appears to be proteolytic degradation of misfolded proteins. Asymmetric damage allocation is also an active strategy, requiring intracellular shuttling, but does not require investment in synthesis, degradation, or extracellular extrusion, and therefore must be (far) less energetically costly, although the cost of asymmetry was not measured directly. This apparent energetic benefit of asymmetric damage allocation comes at a fitness cost: the fitness of one daughter cell, which receives less than half of the somatic damage accumulated by the mother cell, increases at the expense of the other daughter cell which receives more than half.

This tradeoff resulted in the evolution of cell growth strategies including asymmetric allocation of somatic damage across the tree of life. Morphologically asymmetric cell division, in which the asymmetric allocation of cell mass including both resources and damage is apparent after a single cell division, is most thoroughly documented as it can be observed using standard light microscopy, in short-duration experiments. The bacterium Caulobacter crescentus divides morphologically asymmetrically producing one motile and one, immotile, stalk cell. The latter has been shown to age over the course of multiple cell divisions. In the model eukaryote yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, cytoplasmic protein aggregates are actively shuttled away from the smaller “budding” daughter cell. In multicellular tissues, development and homeostasis is achieved through both limited symmetric division of fully differentiated cells and asymmetric division of stem cells resulting in one daughter cell that maintains stemness and another cell that begins to differentiate. In both flies and humans, within both neural and intestinal tissues, somatic damage is asymmetrically allocated to the short-lived lineage [; SI Appendix, Appendix A for further details].

Technological developments in microfluidics and time-lapse microscopy, which enabled tracking many lineages of cells over many cell cycles, revealed that even cells which divide morphologically symmetrically can implement an asymmetric damage allocation strategy. Similarly to C. crescentus (see above), in the morphologically symmetric bacteria Escherichia coli, symmetry breaking between the poles of the cell has been observed. Every pole originates as the result of septum formation during a prior cell division. At the start of each cycle, the cell inherits one new pole and one old pole of variable age. Cells that inherit older poles show increased death rates and decreased growth rates compared to cells inheriting younger poles. As in S. cerevisiae, this effect is primarily attributed to the asymmetric accumulation of protein aggregates.

Similar dynamics have been directly observed in the morphologically symmetric bacteria, in particular, the intracellular pathogen, Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In this system, irreversibly oxidized proteins (IOPs) accumulate under host-induced stress. IOPs are not repaired but asymmetrically allocated between daughter cells at division. Daughter cells which do not receive IOPs have a shorter cell cycle duration on average and reduced mortality following antibiotic exposure. The chaperone ClpB has been shown to facilitate asymmetric allocation whereas the absence of ClpB is associated with reduced fitness in response to environmental stress and reduced virulence in vivo.

The symmetrically dividing model eukaryote, fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, also asymmetrically allocates protein aggregates resulting from both heat and oxidative stress. Although the senescence of this organism remains a matter of debate, asymmetric damage allocation has been demonstrated to be an active process mediated by the Hsp16 chaperone.

Asymmetric damage allocation in morphologically symmetric species can also be environment-dependent. In S. pombe, symmetry breaking is only observed under stress. In E. coli, asymmetric allocation of protein aggregates also becomes more pronounced under stress, for example, heat shock. These findings highlight the phenotypic plasticity of asymmetric allocation as a damage control strategy.

While it is apparent that mechanisms for both repair and asymmetric allocation of somatic damage have evolved across the tree of life, the environmental and physiological determinants of optimal strategy remain poorly understood. Several mathematical modeling approaches have been applied to this problem, the most common one being agent-based simulation. The principal advantage of this approach is the ability to compare relative fitness of agents with selected parameter sets in direct competition, without constructing an absolute fitness function. Charting the global dependence of the somatic damage mitigation strategy on total population size or growth rate, however, remains challenging using this methodology.

We sought to construct a modeling framework to assess the impact of both cell physiology and environmental parameters with respect to an absolute fitness function, namely, the total number of clonal cells. We propose a model of somatic damage accumulation among cells in a chemostat, a stable environment which admits an equilibrium total population size limited by nutrient availability, extrinsic mortality, and somatic damage accumulation. We identify the optimal mitigation strategy, maximizing the total population size, and explore an expansive domain of the parameter space with more than 2.6 million initial conditions where we assume repair, but not asymmetry, to be explicitly growth costly. Within this framework, we find that the optimal strategy is primarily determined by the extrinsic mortality and the physiological model for damage accumulation, consistent with the interpretation that asymmetric damage allocation and repair in unicellular life represent, respectively, r and K selection regimes. We hypothesize that at early stages of cellular evolution, optimization over somatic damage repair and asymmetric allocation played a critical role in establishing repair and asymmetry specialists, driving the evolution of morphologically asymmetric division. This balance of repair and asymmetry, likely an inalienable feature of all life, might represent the prototypical r/K selection strategies which emerged in the earliest cellular organisms.

These periodic solutions were observed relatively rarely, in highly exponential regimes (F ≫ 0). The results of the simulations are described below.
Three Optimal Strategies of Somatic Damage Control.

We first characterized the fitness landscape, that is, the total number of cells at equilibrium with respect to strategy variables in a population adopting the strategy, fixing the remaining parameters (B, D, E, F) which describe environmental conditions and the efficiency of repair. These landscapes can be rugged with multiple local optima, peaks in 3D, separated by valleys of reduced fitness. The largest of these local optima, , represents the optimal strategy under conditions (B, D, E, F). Across all conditions studied, all local optima fall into one of the three categories: i) asymmetry preferred , ii) repair preferred , and iii) combination of strategies . Each of these local optima corresponds to the optimal strategy, , for some parameter set (B, D, E, F). All optima are sensitive to perturbation with respect to both a and r but repair preferred optima are substantially less sensitive to perturbation in a, representing ridges in 3D. Although no local optima were observed for intermediate asymmetry, , can be nonmonotonic with respect to a. The existence of local optima corresponding to intermediate asymmetry depends on the functional form of the death rate due to somatic damage accumulation, , as well as the assumption that asymmetry is not explicitly growth costly (see SI Appendix, Fig. S3 for a landscape with globally optimal intermediate asymmetry under a different model). Consequently, intermediate asymmetry can be observed within natural systems (Discussion). All three types of local optima can be represented within the landscape for a single parameter set (B, D, E, F); however, the most common landscapes observed encompass a single optimum. Examining the population structure at each of the three possible local optima provides more detailed insight into the fitness effects of asymmetric damage allocation and repair (Fig. 2). A naive population (adopting the strategy) has a broad diagonal structure in which cells inherit, on average, the same amount of damage as they will accumulate over the course of one cell cycle. It follows that dividing cells contain approximately twice the amount of damage as newborn cells. The effect of asymmetry and repair on the population structure strongly depends on the model of somatic damage accumulation which can be characterized by the relative impact, , of the linear component of somatic damage on the total population size. When I = 1 (F = 0), somatic damage accumulation is linear; as I→0, somatic damage accumulation becomes exponential (see Methods for computation of I). Asymmetry preferred strategies subdivide the population into several parallel trajectories with different trajectories that represent cells inheriting different amounts of damage. When I ≪ 1, the survival probability of cells that inherit any amount of damage can be low and only the first trajectory can be substantially represented. In contrast, a repair preferred strategy homogenizes the damage distribution with respect to cell size. This observation suggests that repair preferred strategies should be observed more frequently when I ≪ 1 (see below). A combination of strategies unites the effects of subdivision and homogenization, generating a subpopulation with a lower probability of death due to damage accumulation than in a symmetric population with the same investment in repair. The associated cost is the generation of subpopulations with a higher probability of death.

Determinants of Optimal Strategy Represent r/K Selection.

After analyzing the range of possible local optima, we explored the environmental and physiological determinants of globally optimal strategy, , parameterized by (B, D, E, F). Increasing repair efficiency, E, increases both the size of this triangle and the fraction occupied by the repair preferred strategy. Within each triangle, the repair preferred region covers an area of reduced damage accumulation and extrinsic mortality compared to the asymmetry preferred region. Increasing F decreases the size of the triangle, as well as the fraction occupied by the asymmetry preferred strategy, and increases the fraction occupied by the combination of strategies.

While intrinsic mortality depends on multiple parameters, extrinsic mortality is specified explicitly by B. Globally, increasing B leads to an increase of the portion of the region where occupied by the asymmetry preferred strategy. Investment in repair, which is growth costly, increases the probability of cell death due to extrinsic factors per cell cycle. This trend represents a form of r/K selection, a framework within evolutionary ecology that describes the trade-off between offspring number and quality. The repair preferred strategy is a K-strategy, producing high-quality offspring, with low rates of intrinsic mortality, at a low growth rate. The asymmetry preferred strategy is an r-strategy, producing offspring of variable quality, some with high rates of intrinsic mortality, at a high growth rate. As is typical of r/K selection, the asymmetry preferred r-strategy is more commonly observed when the extrinsic mortality rate is high, and intrinsic mortality has a reduced impact on the probability of cell death per cell cycle.
Optimal Strategy Bifurcates Depending on the Model of Damage Accumulation.

Unlike extrinsic mortality, intrinsic mortality depends on multiple parameters, including the strategy parameters (a, r). Consequently, the dependence of the optimal strategy on the intrinsic mortality is complex. We began assessing this dependence at the edge of the region where , that is, the extinction boundary. Consider the ratio of the intrinsic and extrinsic mortality rates for a naive population, , which we denote “harshness”, H (see Methods for details). Increasing F, the exponential component of somatic damage accumulation, increases H at the extinction boundary (Fig. 4A). It follows that for equally challenging initial conditions, as reflected by equal values of H, a combination of somatic damage mitigation strategies incorporating both repair and asymmetry is more likely to prevent population collapse when somatic damage accumulates nonlinearly. This effect is a consequence of the fact that under a linear regime, the rate of damage accumulation does not depend on the mitigation strategy but under a nonlinear regime, this rate is reduced through mitigation.

Discussion

Somatic damage accumulation is an inevitable consequence of cellular metabolism. When the rate of damage accumulation exceeds the rate at which it is diluted through cell growth and division, a dedicated mitigation strategy is required to prevent population collapse. These mitigation strategies can be coarsely divided into two categories: repair and asymmetrical damage allocation. Repair requires the synthesis of replacement materials for the essential cellular machinery or transfer of the dysfunctional material into the external environment. Asymmetry requires intracellular mass transfer so that, upon division, daughter cells receive different amounts of damage. The most common form of somatic damage appears to be the accumulation of misfolded proteins which may be repaired through proteolytic degradation or asymmetrically shuttled and aggregated. Other forms of somatic damage are diverse, as are repair and shuttling mechanisms observed among both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, including multicellular organisms. Investment in dedicated somatic damage mitigation is costly. Under the conceptual framework adopted in this work, repair is explicitly growth-costly whereas asymmetric damage allocation is not. However, asymmetric allocation reduces the fitness of the daughter cell that receives more than half of the somatic damage accumulated by the mother cell. In addition to mechanisms that limit the accumulation of genetic damage, somatic damage mitigation likely plays a central role in the stabilization of unicellular populations and tissue homeostasis in multicellular organisms.

In some systems, a positive association between accumulated damage and stress tolerance has been reported. This observation motivates the hypothesis that misfolded protein aggregates might be used by unicellular organisms as a form of long-term memory to record previously encountered stressors such that the repair machinery preferentially segregates along with the aggregates. Under these conditions, asymmetric allocation of somatic damage would provide both competitive advantages and disadvantages to the cell inheriting the majority of the damage, the balance of which would depend on the environment in a manner not reflected by our current model, motivating future work.

We developed and analyzed a generalizable mathematical model for cell growth, division, and somatic damage mitigation aiming to elucidate the dependence of the optimal strategy on four key variables: i) extrinsic, somatic damage-independent, mortality, ii) efficiency of repair, iii) rate of somatic damage accumulation, and iv) model of damage accumulation, ranging from linear to exponential. We simulated the growth of a population of clonal cells in a chemostat until pseudoequilibrium conditions were met. In order to completely describe the dependence of the damage mitigation strategy on these four factors subject to computational limitations, our framework introduces flexibility with respect to these parameters at the cost of three principal limiting constraints. First, we determine optimal strategy through maximization of an absolute fitness function, the average total number of cells in the population at pseudoequilibrium. This approach does not differentiate between true equilibria and periodic orbits or limit cycles and does not admit the evaluation of direct competition between pairs of strategies. Nor does it admit evaluation of trade-offs between stability and adaptability which are affected by nongenetic heterogeneity, and it follows, by asymmetry. Second, we assume that asymmetry is not growth costly. By varying repair efficiency, this admits the exploration of conditions where the cost of repair is arbitrarily low, but not conditions where asymmetry is more costly than repair. As described in Results, this also impacts our observation that intermediate asymmetry is never optimal within our framework: even under conditions where a combination of strategies is optimal, asymmetry is maximal, combined with repair. While consistent with other studies, this finding is highly model-dependent. These assumptions further do not admit the exploration of conditions where the cost of asymmetric allocation of damage between daughter cells depends on the amount of damage allocated. Third, we introduce extrinsic mortality through dilution of the chemostat which is coupled to nutrient availability.

These constraints did not, however, limit our model agreement with prior efforts. Although not ubiquitously reported, our model reproduces the central result obtained through both diverse theoretical models and experimental inference, that increasing the rate of somatic damage accumulation tends to increase asymmetric allocation. To our knowledge, this result has been previously obtained only for models in which somatic damage accumulates linearly. Indeed, we observed the same behavior when damage accumulation is linear or approximately linear; however, when damage accumulates strongly nonlinearly, the dynamics are more complex.

Although direct measurements of the rate of somatic damage accumulation in single cells remain challenging, model biophysical systems display substantial nonlinearity. In particular, protein misfolding and aggregation typically follow a “seeding-nucleation” model in which early stages are thermodynamically unfavorable until a stable aggregate is formed at which point growth becomes exponential. Similar dynamics are observed over a wide range of model systems including hemoglobin gelation as well as aggregation of ovalbumin and lactic dehydrogenase. When seed formation, that is, de novo misfolding, is the rate-limiting step, these dynamics are linear, but when aggregation becomes rate-limiting, the shift to the exponential regime.

When comparing linear and nonlinear conditions that are equally challenging with respect to the fitness of naive cells or those adopting the optimal strategy for each condition, we observed that nonlinear conditions are less likely to result in population collapse and that in this case, the optimal strategy for damage control is more likely to be dominated by repair. This effect appears to be a consequence of the fact that, under strongly nonlinear conditions, damage accumulation rate is more robustly modifiable through investment in repair. In addition to mutually exclusive repair and asymmetry preferred mitigation strategies, a combination of strategies including both investment in repair and maximal asymmetric allocation is also observed for these conditions of nonlinear damage accumulation. Indeed, this combination of strategies, which generates a subpopulation of cells that inherit no damage upon division through asymmetric damage allocation but also reduces the rate of damage accumulation through investment in repair, is always optimal when the model of damage accumulation is strongly nonlinear. Under these conditions, increasing the linear rate of damage accumulation (e.g., via an uncorrelated environmental stressor) bifurcates the optimal strategy into either asymmetry preferred when extrinsic mortality is high or repair preferred when extrinsic mortality is low. Demonstrating the dependence of optimal somatic damage mitigation strategy on extrinsic mortality is a principal finding of this work. The r/K selection theory categorizes reproductive strategies with respect to the trade-off between maximizing the total number of progeny (r-strategies) and producing (relatively) fewer but higher quality offspring (K-strategies). Subject to the maximum number of individuals the environment can support, K, and the maximum growth rate of the population, r, the population grows according to the rate equation:

When extrinsic mortality is high, N ≪ K and r-strategists prevail; the converse is true when extrinsic mortality is low. Unicellular organisms that employ r-strategies tend to have relatively short cell cycle durations but lower metabolic efficiency, admitting a phase of rapid growth that can be followed by a gradual decline resulting from competition with more efficient K-strategists. Specific genomic determinants of metabolic flexibility and efficiency commonly associated with r- and K-strategies have been identified at variable evolutionary depths. In contrast, relatively little prior work has focused on the study of generalizable division strategies which might be realized among genetically divergent species, as has been explored in greater depth in the related area of cell size regulation.

The relationship between growth and efficiency is complex. In microorganisms, the growth rate is strongly cell-density dependent. As observed in our model, this dependence couples r- and K-strategies, and can result in covariance with respect to changing metabolic strategy rather than a trade-off. In this work, we demonstrate that somatic damage repair, a K-strategy, is favored when the extrinsic mortality rate is low whereas asymmetric damage allocation, an r-strategy, is favored when this rate is high. Both strategies are employed by the same extant prokaryotes and eukaryotes and were likely accessible to the earliest cellular organisms. Optimization over somatic damage repair and asymmetric damage allocation played a critical role in establishing repair and asymmetry specialists including the evolution of morphologically asymmetric division. The balance between repair and asymmetry in early cellular life might represent the prototypical r/K selection regime and perhaps the origin of specialized r/K strategists. Furthermore, it appears likely that asymmetric damage allocation, an r-strategy which remains ubiquitous among cellular life today, was the first damage mitigation strategy to evolve in primordial cells that were likely less robust than modern cells and subject to high extrinsic mortality.

Finally, it is worth briefly discussing how the damage mitigation dynamics shift when somatic damage is externalized, admitting damage accumulation from the environment. When damage is externalized, the rate of damage accumulation is, essentially, linearized. When damage is not externalized, linearization increases the relative fitness of asymmetry preferred strategies; however, when damage is externalized, the asymmetrically allocated damage can be reintroduced via environmental transfer whereas repaired damage cannot. Within our framework, we observed that the landscape for externalizable damage did not substantially differ from what is discussed in the main text, apparently balancing these opposing influences (SI Appendix, Fig. S6). Viral infection represents a specific, strongly nonlinear form of externalizable somatic damage accumulation. Unicellular organisms have evolved a wide range of diver antiviral defense systems to prohibit virion cell entry or destroy viruses intracellularly. One common mechanism by which cells remove viruses from the population is through programmed cell death (PCD). Asymmetric damage allocation is similar to PCD in that one daughter cell attains a state of reduced fitness (and can die if the damage level is high) relative to competitors that divide symmetrically under the same conditions. In contrast to typical PCD, the other cell attains increased fitness. In the strongly nonlinear regime of viral infection, the results presented here suggest that combinations of damage mitigation strategies should be common, suggesting that PCD is even more widespread in unicellular life forms than presently realized.
Methods
Model Construction.

In this section, we describe how we arrived at the master equation presented in the main text from a series of models of increasing complexity, motivating that if the framework studied in this work were to be further simplified, it would be insufficient to represent the biological phenomena of interest. We begin with a continuum description of a cell population of uniform somatic damage concentration. This model is further developed to admit nonuniform somatic damage, reflecting asymmetric allocation. This form, in turn, is developed to enforce a minimum cell size at the time of division. Finally, the discrete master equation is presented to address to address computational concerns.

We begin with the description of the chemostat and an idealized cell population in which the somatic damage concentration is the same for all individuals at any time. The chemostat, of volume V, contains cell media with dissolved nutrients, concentration . Volume is removed per unit time and replaced with fresh cell media (concentration , increasing the nutrient concentration at rate ). Cell mass is measured in units of nutrient. Without investment in repair (asymmetry is assumed not to be growth costly), volume of media is ingested per unit cell mass, per unit time, and 100% of the available nutrient in that volume is converted to cell mass. Investment in repair, R, decreases this fraction proportionately. Cell volume-mass ratio, x, is invariant. So defined, the growth rate for the total cell volume in the chemostat is and the removal of nutrient from the environment reduces the nutrient concentration at rate .

While cell growth can be defined with respect to a unit cell volume, cell loss is defined with respect to individual cells. However, although the average volume per individual cell can be a time-dependent quantity, when somatic damage concentration is the same for all individuals, the probability of cell loss is independent of individual cell volume. Thus, it is possible to describe the rate of the total cell volume loss, without loss of generality.

A fraction of cells are removed from the chemostat, representing extrinsic mortality which, by definition, does not depend on somatic damage accumulation. Intrinsic mortality is determined by accumulated somatic damage.
